ac0cbbd3880d: Eight court sessions, six registers and an admission of seduction were boiled down in the prison to two almost identical entries, one in the register of inmates and one in the class register: since the summer of 1911 he had several times had intercourse with his stepdaughter Kristine Oline Enevoldsen and made her pregnant. <t1>Intercourse</t1> — that is all the register writes, and the relation of power goes unsaid. Even her suspended sentence is reduced to a subordinate clause in the column.
1a50caac9fae: And the words <t1>hard labour in the house of correction</t1> should not be heard with modern ears. Vridsløselille was built on the isolation principle of the Philadelphia system, and in 1913 it was still in force: the sentence was served in a single cell, where the prisoner both worked and slept. Outside the cell the prisoners wore masks so that they could not recognise one another, all conversation was forbidden, and in church and school they sat in small stalls from which they could see the pastor and the teacher — but not each other. The mask was only made voluntary in 1924. In return the Penal Code of 1866 gave a reduction in the term for serving in a cell — the isolation was itself reckoned an aggravation of the punishment, and the time was reduced accordingly. [S118]

8aedf4ff7e92: The eighteen-month sentence ended in release after a good six and a half months served — and the way there took two attempts. The first was the defence counsel’s. In July attorney <t1>Kamp</t1> applied for a pardon for his client; the judge — the same district bailiff who had given the judgment — recommended the petition in a statement of 7 July, and the county passed it on to the Ministry of Justice with the remark that it could refer to the statement given. The ministry’s answer came ten days later, typewritten and short: [S167, S168]
e425f84c9db4: In consequence of this, it is hereby communicated for your kind information and further notice, also to attorney Kamp, that the Ministry <t1>does not find grounds to seek any pardon</t1> for the person concerned.

5a8f4f0bba6c: The refusal was passed on and entered in the institution’s journal. There the case could have ended: judgment, refusal, sentence served to April 1914. But 15 November 1913 was the fiftieth anniversary of the House of Glücksburg on the throne: Christian IX had become king on 15 November 1863, and although he had died in 1906, his grandson Christian X marked the day as the royal line’s jubilee — the prison’s journal itself calls it <t1>“the Lyksborg 50 years’ jubilee of the reign”</t1>. On 10 November Vridsløselille recommended seven prisoners for pardon on that occasion. Prisoner no. 240 was one of them, and the institution’s letter gives the reason: [S169, S170]
2a36cc485cca: He behaves well and seems to repent his crime. <t1>At home he is sorely missed</t1>, and the judge has recommended a petition for pardon, which was refused on 17 July this year, though with reference to the judge’s recommendation.
12629b1deb94: Vridsløselille to the Director of the Prison Service · letter no. 131, 10 November 1913 [S170]
f197dd58a005: The same letter sums up his family in the prison’s own language: <t1>“married and has 3 legitimate children, 1 illegitimate child, 1 child of incest and 3 stepchildren”</t1>. The child of incest is Arne, and the stepchildren are Kristiane’s three children of her first marriage. But whom the letter counts as the illegitimate child remains open: Kristen was born in 1904, two years before his parents’ wedding — but if he is counted as the illegitimate child, the three legitimate children do not add up with the two younger ones, Anna and Niels; and if he was counted as legitimate by the marriage, the letter counts a child the sources otherwise do not know. Nielsine’s child cannot be meant — when the letter was written on 10 November, Else Margrethe was not yet born. The royal resolution came on the anniversary itself, 15 November: all seven pardoned, the three foreign prisoners with expulsion from the realm, all released the same day. At four o’clock he walked out of the gate — not because anyone had changed their view of the case, but because the royal house had been on the throne for fifty years.<t2>?</t2><n1/> [S169, S170]

894ed4556e70: And then the thing no register explains. In February 1913 he declared in court that it had been his intention never to return to his wife. Yet we find them together again: the family reunited on Gl. Færgevej in Esbjerg, Elna born in 1919, and Kristiane as <t1>Mrs Silkjær</t1> at Havnegade 179 right up to 1951 (chapter 11). When and how they were reconciled, there is no source for. It is the last, unwritten sentence of the case — and they wrote it themselves, without a register.

a7271cdc04c3: The prisoner’s fear was well founded. Nielsine was pregnant when he was arrested — the date of birth is consistent with the child having been conceived during the stay in Copenhagen, around the time shortly before the arrest.
beee134c0d66: She did not give birth at home at Årgab. She gave birth in Aarhus — and the parish register records her as an <t1>“unmarried servant girl”</t1>: she was in service in the town, so the journey there was not only a flight to hide. The birth took place at <t2>Bethesda</t2> — a rescue and maternity home for unmarried pregnant women, founded in 1894 and run on Inner Mission funds, with a deaconess as matron. The home cared precisely for the <t3>“fallen for the first time”</t3>, as the period called them: young women expecting a child without a husband, who had few other places to give birth. In 1913 it lay on Skovvangsvej on Aarhus Mark, with room for twenty women and thirty children. [S129]
3e24c4e728b2: It is worth pausing at what that means. The mission movement appears twice in this case, and both times on the same side: through the itinerant preacher Kristine Oline wrote to — the Danish Missionary Society’s man, cf. caveat 35 — and through the Inner Mission’s institutional network, which gave Nielsine a place to give birth. The revival’s people in those years were not only the moral authority that put a name to sin; they were also the social safety net that caught those sin left behind. <t1>“Fallen girl”</t1> is the period’s phrase, not the chronicle’s — but the help was real enough.

4116cfe4d38e: The girl was named after her maternal grandmother and baptised in St John’s Church on 14 December; among the godparents stood <t1>Johanne Nielsen</t1> — most probably Nielsine’s sister, four years older. The family was there, at the font in Aarhus too. And then the date again: <t2>on 15 November 1913, at four o’clock in the afternoon, Thomas walked out of the gate at Vridsløselille</t2>. His second child that year was born on the same day he was freed. So in 1913 he stood in two parish registers as named father — Arne in May at Haurvig, Else Margrethe in November in Aarhus — two children with two women in under six months. Arne was born while he sat in Ringkjøbing jail; Else Margrethe on the day he was released from Vridsløselille. [S44, S125]
e945cb3014ab: Nielsine took the child home to Årgab. In the census of 1916 Else Margrethe appears as a <t1>foster child</t1> with her grandparents — the same discreet column Arne later had in his father’s household — in 1921 simply as <t2>child</t2>. In 1930 they both lived there — Nielsine unmarried and forty-three, her daughter seventeen. Nielsine later had children with another man, and the chronicle follows her no further: that story is hers.
21f241ee4ce9: The daughter grew up on the dunes. She went into service as a <t1>domestic help</t1> and lived in Hvide Sande, a couple of miles from Årgab. On <t2>10 November 1938</t2>, five days before her twenty-fifth birthday, she died at the <t3>mental hospital in Viborg</t3>. The death certificate gives bronchopneumonia as the cause of death and at the same time records “morbus mentalis” — mental illness — without a closer diagnosis. The certificate tells no more. She was unmarried.
686d1796d734: At the top of the certificate someone has written where she was to go: <t1>Nørre Haurvig churchyard</t1>. It is the church on the dunes — the one her half-brother Arne had been carried into as a baby in June 1913, five months before she herself was born in Aarhus. The two never met in any document. They ended in the same parish. [S125, S133]

f6395c6fed51: The prisoner was brought before the court and states that his full name is Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and that he was born on 10 Jan 1882 in Husby, and he denies having previously been charged or punished. The deponent married in 1906 his wife, the widow of fisherman Chr. Enevoldsen, Christiane Enevoldsen, with whom he has 3 children aged 8, 6 and 2 years. There has been nothing wrong in the relationship between his wife and him, and the marriage has until now been particularly happy until last summer, when the deponent began the connection with the daughter of the neighbour Tyge Nielsen, with whom he went away from home in the month of December and has since lived together. When his wife discovered this love affair and could in general feel that the prisoner was not towards her as he had been before, she reproached him for the relationship, without this however bringing any change for the better. Any real rift in the relationship between him and his wife there has not, however, been.
2837b2e75b41: Confronted with the incestuous relationship with his stepdaughter Kristine Oline Enevoldsen of which he is now accused, he admits that he has had intercourse many times with his stepdaughter, whom he has now made pregnant. The relationship began in the summer of 1911, when, as the daughter stated in report A, he had intercourse with her for the first time one evening at harvest time, though he cannot give the time more exactly. It took place in the barn of his property at Aargab. [The record here describes the first occasion and the acts in physical detail, together with his assertion that she went with him willingly and without threats or violence on his part; that passage is not translated.] After that the prisoner had intercourse with her a few more times before 1 Nov. that year, when the daughter went into service, at any rate in her room; after the daughter came home from service on 1/4 1912 the prisoner often had intercourse with her, always in her room. [A further physical detail is not translated.] He states that his stepdaughter always gave herself to him willingly and without any trace of compulsion on his part, which the prisoner of course was clear was in the highest degree wrong. <t1>The prisoner must admit that his stepdaughter drew his attention to the danger in their relationship, but that he always brushed it aside and reassured his stepdaughter that it did not matter, as long as the relationship did not get out among strangers.</t1>
817940f25e4a: It may well be right, as stated by the stepdaughter, that the last intercourse between them took place in the month of August last year. With the girl with whom he went away, Nielsine Nielsen, the prisoner has also had intercourse several times, in particular also during the time when they lived as neighbours on the dunes, which always took place in Nielsine’s room at her parents’. Asked, the prisoner says he has not had physical relations with other women. Read out and confirmed. The prisoner was led away.
252d17b5f8d1: <t1>Blodskamsforhold</t1>, incestuous relationship, is the register’s word. Corrections in the clerk’s own hand have been smoothed out in the transcription; see caveat 32. The reading of the untranslated detail about the occasions in 1912 follows the criminal file’s certified transcript — in the examination of 22 March, on the other hand, he confirmed his stepdaughter’s contrary statement; the contradiction stands in the sources themselves.
